[Rating: 1/10] We tried this at Essen and then played it again just to see if we had missed something.  We had not. The price gains and losses net out to zero every game and there is no way to predict when it will happen.  Just really bad.

[Rating: 1/10] This is one of the worst "games" I have ever played, and by calling it a game im stretching the very definition af a game.  Stay away from this.

[Rating: 1/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  We quite after 8 rounds as we saw little purpose or strategy to this one. Very luck driven with very little in the way of decision making.

[Rating: 1/10] We aborted 6 or 7 rounds in...almost all luck in how the cards come out...it's usually pretty obvious which one to buy and everyone goes for it so they're only available if the person before you was forced to sell it since you HAVE to buy something each round (and you can't buy something you sold of course:) ).

[Rating: 1/10] I logged in just comment. I've played some pretty questionable games throughout my years but this is hands down the worst I've ever seen. I'm not entirely sure who was willing to bankroll this and get it to market in the first place. They must have had about as much business sense as it takes to trade three different cores cubes ad nauseam.

[Rating: 1/10] oh woooooow what a disappointment. Played in BGA, no need to play anywhere else, ever.

[Rating: 1/10] This game is so bad I am considering reworking all of my game ratings so that this is the absolute lowest score I've given.   It is a sum zero market. Every good will return to its initial value by the end of the game. With these bumps up and down being random, the average result is that each good will only ever be worth 1 or 2 dollars more or less than it started.   The game is 27 rounds long. It doesn't matter how fast you play, that is an impossibly hard sell to try to get anyone to play this with you.   Boring. It is a 27 round, random, BORING market game. [Rating: 2/10] Imagine Hab und Gut but suck out all the fun and add in all of the problems they took out with playtesting.  Each stock can move a maximum of 1 up or down a round. This makes it very slow and you are trying to inch profits out as money is so tight.  Also, as the stock movement is completely random (you draw a card with the movements) the only control you have is buying and selling, but with barely any swing on stock prices from round to round, this it pretty boring.  We were very disappointed when we tried this at Essen 2015.

[Rating: 2/10] I'm so, so sad that I have to award the game this low rate. But there's nothing here save speculation with a fixed constraint that prices of gems end up where they started out from. So basically if you know that a gem value has had its value increased by 5 because of 5 succesive increments, you also know that for the remainder of the draw deck cards which lower that amount will appear more frequently... but not [i]when[/i]. [Rating: 2/10] Intriguing buy/sell concept, but slow gameplay, and not enough to do. You are often forced into situations where you have no choice. It's hard to actually make investments, since you always need to buy something; so you usually also need to always sell something, and price fluctuations are glacial.

[Rating: 2/10] This is the weirdest stock game I've ever played.   The market is 100% random, as it is controlled by a deck of cards...NOT the buying and selling of players.   You *have* to buy each round...which sometimes forces you into buying things you would not.  The game goes on for 27 rounds of doing the SAME THING over and over!  This is the antithesis of what makes stock games interesting. When to buy, when to sell. Using those options to manipulate prices and screw opponents over.  Market-based games can be sooo much better. This feels like the idea of a game...but it was never playtested to see if
